title: Whisky and Seafood Pairing | Craft Beer School
desc: How to pair whisky with seafood, from Goan fish curry to tandoori pomfret and prawn ghee roast, with the styles that work and the ones that fight.
teaser: Peated whisky and oysters is the famous one. India's coast has better pairings than that.
standfirst: Seafood is delicate, oily or fiery depending on the coast it comes from. Pick a whisky by weight and smoke, not by price. The pairing mostly takes care of itself.
sections:
The first rule of any pairing is weight. A light, flaky fish and a heavy, sherried whisky will not meet in the middle; the whisky simply wins. A rich, oily fish or a buttery prawn dish can carry a fuller dram.

Seafood also brings salt and a little natural sweetness, especially in prawns, crab and lobster. Whisky with fruit or honey notes plays off that sweetness. Smoky whisky plays off char from a grill or tandoor. Those two ideas cover most good seafood pairings.

Keep the pour small, 15 to 30 ml, with water on the side. Whisky at full strength numbs the palate quickly, which defeats the point of pairing it with something delicate.
Delicate fish wants a light whisky

Steamed or lightly fried fish wants a lighter whisky. Think Lowland or Speyside single malts matured mostly in ex-bourbon casks, or a good grain whisky. They bring citrus, green apple and vanilla without heavy oak.

A few Indian matches:

  • Bengali bhapa ilish, hilsa steamed in mustard paste: the mustard heat likes a fresh, fruity whisky with a splash of water.
  • Kerala karimeen pollichathu, pearl spot fish cooked in banana leaf with a spiced masala: a light whisky with a little honey works with the coconut and spice.
  • Bombay duck fry, crisp and salty: a lightly peated or coastal whisky that has a hint of brine.
Smoke for the grill and the tandoor

Peated whisky and oysters is the classic pairing. Plenty of people pour a few drops of a smoky Islay malt straight onto a raw oyster. Most Indian kitchens do not serve raw oysters, but they serve something better for smoke: seafood out of a tandoor.

Tandoori pomfret, grilled prawns or a whole fish cooked over coals has char, smoke and a tangy marinade. A medium peated whisky matches the char without overwhelming the fish. A heavily peated whisky can work too if the marinade is bold. Our guide to peated whisky with smoked food goes further down this road.
Rich curries need a richer whisky

Coastal curries are not shy. Goan fish curry has coconut, kokum or tamarind sourness and dried chilli heat. Mangalorean prawn ghee roast is buttery, red and fierce. Chettinad crab masala carries black pepper and roasted spice.

These dishes need a whisky with body. An ex-bourbon single malt at a slightly higher strength, or a blend with some sherry cask in it, stands up to coconut and ghee. Add water to bring the strength down. Chilli heat and high alcohol together make both feel hotter, so a whisky at around 30 to 35% ABV in the glass is easier going with spicy food than one at 46%.
Sweet casks and tannin fight with fish

A few combinations reliably go wrong:

  • Heavy PX or port cask whiskies with delicate white fish. The sweetness tastes cloying next to the fish.
  • Very tannic, young whisky with oily fish such as mackerel or sardines. Tannin and fish oil can leave a metallic taste.
  • Big peated whisky with steamed or lemony dishes. The smoke has nothing to talk to.

None of these are rules carved in stone. They are the clashes that turn up most often, so they are worth testing deliberately once rather than finding by accident at a dinner.
Shellfish likes a touch of sweetness

Prawns, crab and lobster carry a natural sweetness that fish does not. That sweetness pairs well with whiskies that have honey, vanilla or ripe fruit from ex-bourbon casks. A butter garlic prawn dish with a soft, honeyed single malt is an easy win.

Crab is richer. A Kolkata style crab curry or a pepper crab from the Tamil coast can take a whisky with a little sherry cask influence. The dried fruit meets the sweetness of the crab meat and the spice keeps it from turning heavy. Keep the strength down with water if the dish is hot.

Squid and calamari fried in a light batter go the other way. They want something crisp and lighter so the oil does not double up with a heavy spirit.
Set up a pairing at home

The easiest way to learn is a small side by side. Cook or order two seafood dishes that differ clearly, one delicate and one rich or grilled. Pour two whiskies, one light and fruity, one smoky or richer.

Taste each whisky with each dish and note which combination makes both taste better, which makes one disappear and which clashes. Four combinations teach more than reading a dozen pairing charts. Plenty of water, small pours and nobody drives home afterwards.

Pairing is really applied sensory skill: knowing what is in the glass well enough to predict what it will do next to food. Our guide to whisky and Indian food covers the meat and vegetarian side. Start with one fried fish and two whiskies this weekend.
faqs: Does peated whisky go with seafood?
Yes, especially grilled, smoked or tandoor seafood and raw oysters. It struggles with steamed or very delicate fish.
What whisky goes with spicy fish curry?
A fuller whisky with some body, served with water to bring the strength down. High alcohol makes chilli heat feel hotter.
Should I add water when pairing whisky with food?
Usually yes. A splash of water lowers the alcohol so you can taste the food and opens up the whisky's aroma.
What is the worst whisky and seafood pairing?
Very sweet sherry or port cask whisky with delicate white fish is a common clash. The sweetness swamps the fish.
